title: Myths About American History
objective: After this level you can debunk popular myths, like Washington's cherry tree, and explain how such myths get started and why they last.
summary: Weems invented the cherry tree in 1806, Longfellow’s 1860 poem remade Revere’s ride, and the Betsy Ross flag story surfaced in 1870. Myths come late, with a hero and a lesson.

cards.headline: Young George Washington never confessed to chopping down a cherry tree.
cards.body: The story was invented after he died. Myths aren’t just mistakes: someone made each one, for a reason. Finding the maker is how you debunk it.

cards.headline: The parson’s cherry tree
cards.body: Mason Locke “Parson” Weems published his Washington biography in 1800, a year after Washington’s death. The cherry tree story first appeared in its fifth edition, in 1806, six years later. The book became a bestseller, and school readers retold the story to generations of American schoolchildren. A lesson in honesty, made up.

cards.headline: The midnight ride, retold
cards.body: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow published “Paul Revere’s Ride” in December 1860, as the crisis between North and South grew. He took significant poetic license. William Dawes and Samuel Prescott also rode that night. A British patrol stopped all three: Dawes and Prescott escaped, and Revere was held. Revere never reached Concord, and he did not ride alone.

cards.headline: Betsy Ross’s flag
cards.body: The story that Betsy Ross made the first flag was made public by her grandson William Canby in 1870, in a paper to the Historical Society of Pennsylvania drawing on family stories. There is no firm evidence that she designed or made the first flag. She did make flags for the navy. The family story grew into a national legend.

cards.headline: Why myths last
cards.body: Look at the pattern. Each story appeared long after the event, from someone with a reason: a bestselling biographer, a poet in a nation near war, a proud grandson. Each offered a simple hero and a lesson. Level 11 showed another: the 1621 harvest is commonly called the first Thanksgiving, but Lincoln made Thanksgiving a national holiday only in 1863.

cards.headline: Myths About American History: explained
learned: Weems invented the cherry tree in 1806
Dawes and Prescott rode too; Revere was stopped
The Betsy Ross flag story has no firm evidence
Myths come late, with a hero and a lesson

questions.prompt: Who invented the story of young Washington and the cherry tree?

options.label: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow
options.rationale: Longfellow wrote the 1860 poem about Paul Revere.

options.label: William Canby
options.rationale: Canby told the Betsy Ross story in 1870.

options.label: John Adams
options.rationale: Adams had nothing to do with the story.

questions.explanation: Parson Weems added the cherry tree story to the fifth edition of his Washington biography in 1806.

questions.prompt: A famous story about a Revolutionary hero first appears in a poem written 85 years later. What should a historian do first?

options.label: Accept it, since poems preserve memory
options.rationale: A later poem is not evidence from the time.

options.label: Reject everything about the Revolution
options.rationale: The event may be real even if the details are myth.

options.label: Look for primary sources made at the time of the event
Choose whichever version is more exciting

questions.explanation: Check the story against primary sources from the time; myths like Revere’s lone ride appeared long after the event.

questions.prompt: Like the cherry tree, the “first Thanksgiving” label came later. When did Lincoln make Thanksgiving a national holiday (Level 11)?

options.rationale: That was the harvest celebration itself.
That was the Declaration of Independence.
That was the first National Day of Mourning at Plymouth.

questions.explanation: Lincoln proclaimed Thanksgiving a national holiday only in 1863, long after the 1621 harvest.
